We were driving back from a weekend trip.
The forecast had mentioned some snow, but nothing that sounded serious.
We didn't even think about leaving a day earlier.
About an hour into the drive, the snow started coming down harder than expected.
Within another twenty minutes, the road ahead had basically disappeared into one solid sheet of white.
Cars in front of us slowed to a crawl, then stopped completely.
Pretty soon we were just sitting there, engine running, watching snow pile up on the windshield faster than the wipers could clear it.
I turned on the radio, hoping for some kind of traffic update.
But all I got was static and one very confused local station still playing regular music, like nothing unusual was happening outside at all.
I checked my phone for updates, and honestly, service was barely working.
I could just barely see a message saying the highway was closed a few miles ahead, due to multiple accidents in the storm.
We sat in that line of cars for almost two hours.
We shared half a bag of chips we'd bought at a gas station earlier, and that suddenly felt like the smartest decision we'd made all weekend.
Eventually, a plow came through and slowly cleared one lane.
Cars started inching forward, though "inching" is honestly generous for how slowly we actually moved.
By that point, we'd finished the chips entirely.
We moved on to guessing how many more miles were left, based purely on vague road signs half buried in snow.
That turned out to be a surprisingly bad way to estimate anything.
We ended up pulling off at the first exit we could find.
We checked into a small roadside motel that had exactly one room left.
It felt like winning a small, slightly damp lottery.
The front desk guy barely looked up from his phone as he handed over the key.
He mentioned, casually, that we were actually the third stranded couple to check in that same evening.
It sounded like this happened basically every winter.
We didn't have a single bag with us, no toothbrushes, no change of clothes, nothing.
So we just collapsed onto the bed fully dressed, still slightly damp from the snow, and honestly didn't care even a little.
It was the best kind of tired I'd felt in a long time.
The next morning, the snow had stopped and the roads were cleared.
The whole thing felt almost unreal, like we'd imagined the previous night's chaos while eating gas station chips in a stopped car.
Now I check the forecast obsessively before any winter road trip, and I always keep snacks and a blanket in the trunk, just in case a little snow decides to become something much bigger.
